content.title: About
content.content: Cashews are the edible seeds of the cashew tree (Anacardium occidentale), native to tropical regions of South America and now cultivated in Asia, Africa and the Caribbean. They have a mild, buttery‑sweet flavor and a crunchy texture. Cashews are eaten raw, roasted, or baked, and are used in sauces, pastes, desserts, and plant‑based milks.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The cashew nut hangs from the bottom of a fleshy fruit called the cashew apple, which is also edible.
Unsalted cashews are often sold as whole nuts, but they are sometimes lightly roasted to enhance flavor.
Cashews are a rich source of copper, an essential mineral for iron metabolism and connective tissue formation.
In India, cashews are a key ingredient in traditional sweets such as kaju katli and kaju barfi.
Unlike many other nuts, cashews have a thin skin that is easy to digest.

items.title: High in copper
items.content: Copper in cashews supports red blood cell formation and immune function.

items.title: Contains heart‑healthy monounsaturated fats
items.content: The majority of fat in cashews is monounsaturated, which can help maintain healthy cholesterol levels.

items.title: Source of magnesium and phosphorus
items.content: Magnesium aids muscle and nerve function, while phosphorus is important for bone health.

items.title: Provides plant protein and fiber
items.content: Cashews supply a good blend of amino acids and dietary fiber, promoting satiety and digestive health.

items.title: Rich in antioxidants
items.content: They contain tocopherols and phenolic compounds that help protect cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Tree nut allergy
items.content: Cashews can trigger allergic reactions, including anaphylaxis, in susceptible individuals.

items.title: High calorie density
items.content: Because they are calorie‑dense, portion control is recommended.

items.title: Oxalate content
items.content: People prone to kidney stones may need to limit cashew intake due to oxalates.

items.title: Choking hazard for young children
items.content: Whole cashews are not suitable for children under 4 years old.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Cashews can be enjoyed as a snack, added to salads, oatmeal, yogurt, used in sauces, pastes (cashew butter), baked goods, or made into plant‑based milk. Soaking softens them and makes skin removal easier. Unsalted cashews are a wholesome option.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store cashews in an airtight container in a cool, dry, dark place. For longer shelf life, keep them in the refrigerator or freezer to prevent oil oxidation. Discard nuts that smell rancid or stale.
